intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that split-hand/foot malformation-6 (SHFM6) is caused by homozygous mutation in the WNT10B gene on chromosome 12q13.

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation-6 (SHFM6) is caused by homozygous mutation in the WNT10B gene.
checks.evidence_quote: by subsequent candidate gene approach a homozygous missense WNT10b mutation (p.R332W) in all affected individuals but the atypical case plus in an asymptomatic female
checks.explanation: Abstract reports homozygous WNT10b mutation causing autosomal recessive SHFM; SHFM6 designation is standard nomenclature (also per citing paper [5]).

checks.claim: The WNT10B gene is located on chromosome 12q13.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified by homozygosity mapping a novel SHFM locus at 12q13.11-q13 with a maximum multipoint lod score of 5.47 and by subsequent candidate gene approach a homozygous missense WNT10b mutation
checks.explanation: WNT10b identified within the 12q13 locus; location is standard nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Split-hand/foot malformation (SHFM) is a complex limb malformation that affects the central rays of the autopod (Ugur and Tolun, 2008). It is characterized by absence of the central digital rays, a deep median cleft, and syndactyly of the remaining digits (Gul and Oktenli, 2002). Most familial cases show autosomal dominant inheritance (Gul and Oktenli, 2002). SHFM6 is a rare autosomal recessive form (Ugur and Tolun, 2008; Blattner et al., 2010).

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation (SHFM) is a complex limb malformation that affects the central rays of the autopod.
checks.evidence_quote: Split-Hand/Foot Malformation (SHFM) is a complex limb malformation affecting the central rays of the autopod.

checks.claim: Split-hand/foot malformation is characterized by absence of the central digital rays, a deep median cleft, and syndactyly of the remaining digits.
checks.evidence_quote: Split hand and foot malformation syndrome (SHFM) is characterized by the absence of the central digital rays, deep median cleft, and syndactyly of the remaining digits.

checks.claim: Most familial cases of split-hand/foot malformation show autosomal dominant inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: The majority of the familial cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

checks.claim: SHFM6 is a rare autosomal recessive form of split-hand/foot malformation.
checks.evidence_quote: This is the first reported WNT10b mutation on the pathogenesis of limb development and recessive mutation in SHFM.
checks.explanation: Abstract describes autosomal recessive SHFM and the first recessive mutation, which is consistent with a rare form. The SHFM6 label is standard nomenclature.

checks.evidence_quote: Ray and Freire-Maia also reported autosomal recessive ectrodactyly

(2009) (PMID 21088720) describing PMID 4320415, not the paper's own text; the claim was not checked against PMID 4320415 itself. Verdict on the later paper's description: partially_supported. Only the title was supplied, and it does not mention autosomal recessive inheritance. That reading comes only from later papers that cite Ray, so Ray's own interpretation can't be confirmed.

paragraphs.text: Several reports of affected sibs, some born to consanguineous parents, suggested that split-hand/foot malformation can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait (Ray, 1970; Freire-Maia, 1971; Verma et al., 1976; Mufti and Wood, 1987).

checks.claim: Several reports of affected sibs, some born to consanguineous parents, suggested that split-hand/foot malformation can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
checks.evidence_quote: This report, together with those of Ray (1960) and Freire-Maia (1971), further demonstrates that split-hand and -foot deformity can be inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
checks.explanation: The paper reports affected sibships born to consanguineous parents and concludes that inheritance can be autosomal recessive. This supports the paper's part of the multi-citation claim. Note that the paper dates Ray's report to 1960, while the draft cites Ray, 1970. That citation is not part of this claim's substance, but it is worth checking.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora and Nubani (1989) discussed whether their family represented a rare autosomal recessive form of SHFM. As an alternative, they proposed a 2-locus model in which a dominant SHFM mutation is controlled by a gene at another locus, and a dominant mutation at that controlling locus causes the SHFM mutation to be nonpenetrant. Gul and Oktenli (2002) discussed both autosomal recessive inheritance and a 2-locus model for their inbred kindred.

checks.explanation: The abstract discusses a possible rare autosomal recessive form in connection with this family.

checks.explanation: The abstract describes the 2-locus model in the same way. The abstract says the paper discussed the model; calling it 'proposed as an alternative' is a fair paraphrase.

paragraphs.text: Blattner et al. (2010) noted that sporadic SHFM is generally thought to result from new dominant mutations. They showed that sporadic SHFM can instead be recessive. In that case, the recurrence risk is 25% for sibs rather than very low, and the risk for offspring of patients is very low unless there is consanguinity, rather than an estimated 30 to 50%. They recommended that patients with sporadic SHFM be tested for mutations in WNT10B to determine the recurrence risk.

paragraphs.text: Ugur and Tolun (2008) used a candidate gene approach within the 12q13 locus in a large consanguineous Turkish kindred with autosomal recessive SHFM. They identified a homozygous missense mutation in the WNT10B gene (R332W). It was present in all affected individuals except the one with atypical SHFM, and also in 1 asymptomatic female. In the TP63 gene, they found a rare insertion variant (rs34201045) in most affected individuals. This variant lies at the alternate promoter used for transcription of the N-terminally truncated p63 isoform.

paragraphs.text: In an Indian girl with SHFM, sparse hair, and interrupted eyebrows, Kantaputra et al. (2018) identified a homozygous 3-bp deletion in the WNT10B gene (c.695_697delACA). The deletion is predicted to remove a single residue in frame (Asn232del). Protein modeling suggested that losing this residue at a critical position would severely disrupt protein structure and function. They suggested it would likely shorten the protein's lifetime and prevent binding to its receptors and other ligands.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a large consanguineous Turkish kindred with autosomal recessive SHFM6, Ugur and Tolun (2008) identified a homozygous arg332-to-trp (R332W) mutation in the WNT10B gene. They found it by homozygosity mapping followed by a candidate gene approach. The mutation was present in all affected individuals except 1 with an atypical, mild phenotype, and also in 1 asymptomatic female. The authors proposed that either a second locus contributes to the phenotype or a suppressor locus prevented the trait from appearing in the nonpenetrant female.
